newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr slips,market scents Japan rate shift.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr slips,market scents Japan rate shift.

text.p: The Australian dollar slid sharply aginst the yen in mid-morning trade after a key economic report from Japan proved much stronger than expected, stirring fears interest rates there may finally be heading higher.

The Bank of Japan's Tankan quarterly survey of business sentiment was far more upbeat than even the most optimistic estimate with the main diffusion index for large manufacturing firms showing a reading of plus 7.0.
Japanese bond yields leapt as a result and US$/yen dropped 3/4 yen in a minute, dragging the local dollar down to 85.41/51 yen from 86.05/15 just ahead of the release.
It was steadier on the U.S. dollar at US$0.7497/02 from an early US$0.7501/06 having already eased from US$0.7518/23 overnight and with the market locked in a tight trading range.
Dealers were not sure this equanimity would last given investors around the world would now have to revise entirely their expectations for Japanese monetary policy this year.

The consensus had been the BOJ would keep rates at a record low until at least the first quarter of 1998 but the Tankan was so strong the risks now favoured a move before year-end. In reaction the December three month Euroyen futures contract dived 13 basis point to 99.02, implying a rate of 0.98 percent.

The March 1998 contract tumbled 16 basis points to 98.78, so implying a rate of 1.22 percent, all of which pointed to the expectation of a hike in the present 0.50 percent discount rate. The impact of the Tankan was all the greater since the market had been lulled by rumours the June survey would be depressed by the economic volatility surrounding a hike in VAT rates in April.

Instead, manufacturing industry seemed to have weathered the disruption remarkably well and were more confident than at any time since 1991. And the improvement was expected to last with the BOJ forecasting a diffusion index of plus 8.0 for Q3.
Data on the real economy were also upbeat with big manufacturers expecting to raise capital spending by 8.5 percent over 1997/98, up from 2.7 percent in the March quarter survey.

The non-manufacturing sector was far less confident, with the diffusion index for big firms at minus 7.0 from minus 6.0 in Q1, although the BOJ predicted an improvement to minus 4.0 in the September survey.

Small firms also remained depressed but that provided little comfort to Japanese debt markets where the benchmark 10-year JGB bond yield climbed 0.125 point to 2.460, so narrowing the wide gap between Japanese and Australian yields.

That gap had already shrunk dramatically in the last year as the Reserve Bank here cut official rates four times to 5.5 percent from 7.5 percent. And the market has been pricing in yet another domestic easing, perhaps as early as next week's RBA board meeting.
Crucially Australian yields at the short end of the curve had moved below those in the U.S., making the A$ less attractive for Japanese investors to hold when compared with the US$.
Rising Japanese bond yields would make it all the harder for the A$ to attract funds, analysts said.
But the implications of the Tankan were not all bearish.
The pickup in economic growth the survey signalled was potentially of great benefit to the dollar since Japan was the single largest consumer of Australian commodities.
And commodities like coal and copper make up over 60 percent of Australia's exports.

Analysts said the relationship was so close that the main Tankan index had a good correlation with the RBA commodity price index, leading it higher and lower over time. The decisive rise in the index seen today, therefore, promised to lead commodity prices higher in the months ahead to the eventual benefit of the dollar. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
